What is Medical Entomology, and why does it matter?

blocks.x: <term d="The scientific study of insects and other arthropods.">Entomology</term> is the study of insects and arthropods, especially those that transmit pathogens to humans. It is one of the core branches of microbiology, alongside bacteriology, virology, mycology, and parasitology.

blocks.title: Why entomology is inseparable from clinical medicine

blocks.x: The majority of the world's most devastating infectious diseases are vector-borne — transmitted by insects and other arthropods. Malaria, filariasis, onchocerciasis, sleeping sickness, dengue, yellow fever, plague, and typhus are all spread by arthropod vectors. Understanding entomology gives clinicians the tools to recognize transmission routes, prevent infection, and interpret epidemiological data.

Vector-borne pathogens span all major microbial groups. Viruses spread this way include dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever, West Nile, and Zika. Bacteria include Yersinia pestis (plague), Borrelia burgdorferi and B. recurrentis, and Rickettsia rickettsii. Parasites include Trypanosoma species, Wuchereria bancrofti, Onchocerca volvulus, and Leishmania species.

sections.title: Phylum Arthropoda: the most successful animals on Earth

blocks.x: Arthropods comprise roughly 85% of all known animal species — over 1 million described species. All arthropods share a common body plan: a tough outer cuticle (exoskeleton), and jointed appendages including legs and antennae.
The phylum splits into several classes of medical relevance:

items: Insecta — the largest class: houseflies, mosquitoes, lice, beetles.
Arachnida — ticks, spiders, mites, scorpions; major disease vectors.
Crustacea — cyclops, crabs, lobsters; some serve as intermediate hosts for parasites.
Diplopoda — millipedes.
Chilopoda — centipedes.

blocks.title: Insects vs. Arachnids — the quick tell

blocks.x: Insects: 3 pairs of legs (6 total), usually 2 pairs of wings, body in 3 parts (head, thorax, abdomen), breathe via tracheae. Arachnids: 4 pairs of legs (8 total), no wings and no antennae, body in 2 parts (prosoma/cephalothorax + opisthosoma/abdomen), breathe via spiracles/stigmata.

Insects owe their extraordinary ecological dominance to five traits: a short life cycle enabling rapid adaptation, adaptability and flight for dispersal, small size minimizing food/shelter needs, high reproductive capacity, and sophisticated sensory systems (chemoreceptors, mechanoreceptors, compound eyes).

sections.title: The medically important insect orders

blocks.x: A handful of insect orders account for almost all arthropod-borne disease:

items: Diptera — mosquitoes, blackflies, sandflies, tsetse flies. Vectors of malaria, filariasis, onchocerciasis, sleeping sickness.
Anoplura — sucking lice. Vectors of typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii) and relapsing fever.
Dictyoptera — cockroaches. Mechanical vectors of enteric pathogens.
Hymenoptera — bees and ants. Significant allergen sources with anaphylaxis risk.

blocks.x: Insects also split by wing development history: <term d="Primitive, wingless insects with no metamorphosis.">Apterygota</term> (wingless, no metamorphosis) versus <term d="Winged insects, further split by how their metamorphosis proceeds.">Pterygota</term> (winged, undergo metamorphosis) — and Pterygota further splits into Exopterygota and Endopterygota by development type, covered next.

sections.title: Exopterygota vs. Endopterygota: two ways to grow up

blocks.x: This distinction is clinically important: <term d="Undergoing complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa and adult.">holometabolousUndergoing complete metamorphosis with a pupal stage: egg, larva, pupa, adult.</term> insects like mosquitoes have larval stages with entirely different habitats and feeding behaviors from adults — informing separate control strategies for each life stage.
Wings develop externally, visible in immature stages. Immature stage is called a nymph. No pupal stage. Examples: lice, cockroaches, grasshoppers.
Wings develop internally during the larval stage. Immature stage is called a larva. Includes a pupal stage. Examples: mosquitoes, flies, beetles, fleas.

In holometabolous vectors like mosquitoes, larvae are aquatic while adults are aerial — meaning larval control (draining stagnant water) and adult control (insecticides, bed nets) must be addressed as two separate problems.

sections.title: Growth in discrete stages: moulting, instars, and metamorphosis

blocks.x: Growth is restricted to immature stages — adults do not grow. The rigid exoskeleton must be periodically shed, a hormone-triggered process called ecdysis (moulting). The old cuticle is digested by moulting fluid and shed along the ecdysial cleavage line; the shed skin is called the exuviae.

items: Instar — each developmental stage or form between moults. Most species have 3–4 larval instars.
Stadium — the time interval spent within one instar.
Eclosion — hatching from the egg.
Metamorphosis — the full transformation from egg to adult.
Imago — the reproductively mature adult stage; no further growth occurs.

blocks.x: After each <term d="To shed the old cuticle in order to grow.">moult</term>, the newly emerged insect swallows air or water to expand its still-soft new <term d="The outer covering or 'skin' of an arthropod.">integument</term> before it hardens — this is one of the key roles of the open blood system, covered next.

sections.title: The blood system: haemolymph and the open circulatory system

blocks.x: Insects have an open circulatory system — there are no true veins or arteries. The body cavity (haemocoel) is filled with haemolymph, a colourless fluid performing the combined functions of blood and lymph.

Haemolymph functions: transports nutrients and hormones, carries excretory products to excretory organs, contains phagocytic haemocytes for immune defense, and participates in clotting and wound repair. Mechanically, it exerts hydraulic pressure — critical for wing expansion after moulting and for eclosion from the pupal case.

The only true blood vessel is the dorsal vessel — a posterior pulsating heart with valve-like ostia openings, and an anterior aorta delivering haemolymph to the brain. The haemocoel is divided into dorsal, perivisceral, and ventral sinuses by two horizontal diaphragms.

sections.title: The respiratory system: breathing without lungs

blocks.x: Insects breathe via a network of internal air tubes — the tracheal system — rather than using a blood-based oxygen carrier. Insects have no haemoglobin; oxygen delivery relies entirely on diffusion.

items: Spiracles — external openings on the meso- and metathoraces and abdominal segments 1–8.
Tracheae — internal tubes conveying air to tissues, reinforced with spiral thickenings to prevent collapse.
Tracheoles — the finest terminal tubes, ending directly in cells for gas exchange.

blocks.x: Spiracle valves open and close to regulate water loss — critical in hot, dry environments — and the system may be partially or fully closed (valved) to conserve moisture.

sections.title: The nervous system and sensory receptors

blocks.x: Three pairs of ganglia in the head fuse to form the brain. The supra-esophageal component coordinates movement and environmental stimuli; the ventral nerve cord projects to all body parts.

Sensory receptors include mechanoreceptors (touch, vibration, hearing — on antennae, wing base, legs), chemoreceptors (taste and smell — antennae, palps), photoreceptors (ocelli and compound eyes), and humidity/temperature receptors (e.g. in lice for host-seeking).
An efficient endocrine system of hormones — including juvenile hormone and ecdysone — regulates growth, moulting, reproduction, and diapause.

sections.title: The digestive system: foregut, midgut, hindgut

blocks.x: The insect gut shows enormous diversity matching the variety of food types consumed — sucking mouthparts in mosquitoes versus chewing mouthparts in cockroaches. The alimentary canal has three regions:

items: Foregut — mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → crop (storage) → proventriculus (grinding, straining) → valve (prevents regurgitation).
Midgut — the primary site of digestion and absorption, lined by the protective peritrophic membraneA protective lining of the midgut that prevents abrasion by food particles..
Hindgut — ileum → rectum → anus. Contains Malpighian tubules and rectal papillae, which reabsorb up to 90% of water from the forming faecal pellet.

blocks.x: In blood-sucking insects, saliva is medically critical: anticoagulins prevent clotting, allergens trigger the itch and wheal of bites, and some components have antimicrobial properties.

sections.title: Excretion: maintaining a constant internal environment

blocks.x: The excretory system's primary goal is regulating the pH and osmotic concentration of the haemolymph, achieved mainly through the <term d="Blind-ending tubes at the mid/hindgut junction that extract nitrogenous waste from the haemolymph.">Malpighian tubules</term> — slender, blind-ending tubes at the mid/hindgut junction.

Nitrogen may be excreted as uric acid (most insects — water-conserving), urea, or ammonia depending on species and water availability. The rectum reabsorbs up to 90% of water from the pre-urine — a critical adaptation for surviving in arid environments.

sections.title: Reproductive anatomy and modes of reproduction

blocks.x: Sexes in insects are almost always separate. Mate finding is mediated by pheromones, and fertilization is internal.
Female anatomy: paired ovaries (made of ovarioles), oviducts, a median oviduct/uterus, and a spermatheca — a muscular pouch storing sperm for release over an extended period.

Male anatomy: paired testes producing sperm, vas deferens and seminal vesicle for storage, accessory glands secreting seminal fluid to form the spermatophore, and external genitalia (aedeagus/penis, claspers).
Four modes of reproduction:

items: Oviparous (most common) — eggs laid, develop and hatch externally. E.g. mosquitoes, flies, beetles.
Ovoviviparous — eggs retained internally, hatch inside, larvae emerge fully developed. E.g. some blowflies.
Viviparous — live larvae born directly, nourished internally. E.g. tsetse fly (Glossina) — critical to trypanosomiasis epidemiology.
Parthenogenesis — reproduction from unfertilized ova. E.g. drone bees (arrhenotoky) — workers come from fertilized eggs, drones from unfertilized.

sections.title: Bringing it together

blocks.x: A solid grasp of insect taxonomy, physiology, and life history is essential for understanding how vector-borne pathogens are transmitted, maintained, and controlled. Every subsequent topic — mosquitoes, lice, bedbugs — builds on the foundations covered here: arthropod classification, metamorphosis type, and the internal systems that make insects such effective disease vectors.

lines: Insects: 3 leg pairs, 3 body parts, tracheal breathing
Arachnids: 4 leg pairs, 2 body parts, spiracle/stigmata breathing
Exopterygota: nymph, no <term d="The non-feeding stage in which an insect is reorganised into the adult form.">pupa</term>, external wing buds (lice, cockroaches)
Endopterygota: larva, has pupa, internal wing dev. (mosquitoes, flies, fleas)
Instar = stage between moults | Stadium = time in one instar
Blood: open system, haemolymph, dorsal vessel + ostia
Oviparous (most common) | Ovoviviparous | Viviparous (tsetse) | Parthenogenesis (drone bees)
